issues.legal_issue: A tax imposed by legislation remains subject to the fundamental-rights limitations on valid law.
material_facts: The petitions challenged the constitutionality of a state land-tax statute on the ground that it infringed fundamental rights.
The State argued that the taxing power under Article 265 placed the statute beyond challenge under Part III of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: Article 265 is not a complete answer to a fundamental-rights challenge: authority of law means valid law, and a taxing statute that violates Article 14 is unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Article 265 requires a tax to be imposed and collected under valid law. Validity requires both legislative competence and compliance with Article 13, including the prohibition in Article 13(2) against laws abridging fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.tax_law_challenged_as_infringing_fundame: A person challenged a tax law on the ground that it infringed fundamental rights.

issues.definition: When a tax law is challenged in a constitutional petition for infringing fundamental rights, the law remains subject to those fundamental-rights limits.

issues.legal_issue: A uniform land tax that makes no classification by relevant differences in the land can deny equality when it imposes unequal burdens on holders of land.
material_facts: The statute imposed the same flat tax rate on all lands, whatever their description or tenure.
The tax did not account for the land’s quality, productive capacity, or actual or potential income.
The petitioners’ forest lands included areas that yielded little income, while the tax was payable regardless of whether the land produced income or could produce it.
issues.conclusion: The flat-rate levy lacked a classification that prevented unequal burdens on holders of land and infringed Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxing statutes. Different classes of property may be taxed differently on a rational basis, but a law may violate equality where the absence of classification creates inequality among holders of the same kind of property. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar for the principle that a statute conferring unguided selection discretion may itself create discrimination.

rule.if: constitutional_rights_petition and land_tax_challenge and uniform_tax_ignores_land_productivity and no_relevant_property_classification

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.land_tax_challenge: A person challenged a law that imposes tax on land.
predicates.uniform_tax_ignores_land_productivity: The law imposes a uniform tax on land without accounting for differences in its productive capacity or income.
predicates.no_relevant_property_classification: The law makes no relevant classification among the properties or holders subject to the tax.

issues.definition: A land-tax scheme denies equal protection when, in a constitutional challenge, it uniformly taxes land without regard to productivity and makes no relevant classification.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to exempt land from a tax without guiding principles is discriminatory, and an integral exemption provision cannot be severed from the rest of the statute.
material_facts: The statute empowered the government to exempt any land or class of lands, wholly or partly, from the tax by notification.
The statute set out no principle or policy to guide the government’s choice of which lands or classes to exempt.
The exemption power and the charging provisions were treated by the Court as main provisions of the statute.
issues.conclusion: The exemption power infringed Article 14, and it was not severable from the rest of the statute.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits a statute from delegating uncontrolled selection power that allows discrimination between similarly situated persons or things. Under Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, a court examines whether the statute provides a principle or policy to guide the selection; without one, the statutory discretion is arbitrary. The Court held that severance was unavailable because the charging provisions and exemption provision were main provisions of the statute.

rule.if: constitutional_rights_petition and tax_exemption_power and exemption_power_unguided and exemption_power_integral_to_tax_scheme

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.tax_exemption_power: A tax law authorizes the government to exempt property or classes of property from the tax.
predicates.exemption_power_unguided: The law provides no principle or policy to guide the government’s choice of exemptions.
predicates.exemption_power_integral_to_tax_scheme: The exemption power is a main and integral part of the tax scheme.

issues.definition: An unguided exemption power in a constitutional challenge is invalid and cannot be severed when it is integral to the tax scheme.

issues.legal_issue: A tax scheme that permits conjectural provisional assessments without adequate assessment procedures or an ascertainable deadline for regular assessment can impose unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property.
material_facts: The statute authorized provisional tax assessments for unsurveyed land and made the assessed amount payable.
It prescribed no machinery or procedure for making the assessment, including no required notice, process for correcting errors, or appeal.
It imposed no prescribed or ascertainable period within which the government had to survey the land and make a regular assessment.
The petitioners’ forest use was restricted, and the illustrative forest owner’s stated annual income was substantially below the tax demanded on the provisional assessment.
issues.conclusion: The provisional-assessment provision imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property protected by Article 19(1)(f); the Court also held that the operative provisions had a confiscatory effect and offended that guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protected the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property. The Court treated tax assessment as at least quasi-judicial and held that a provision allowing repeated provisional assessments on a conjectural basis, without prescribed assessment safeguards or a time limit for regular assessment, imposed unreasonable restrictions. It also relied on the practical effect of the tax burden in concluding that the operative provisions were confiscatory and infringed Article 19(1)(f).

rule.if: constitutional_rights_petition and property_tax_assessment_challenge and provisional_assessment_payable and assessment_procedure_absent and regular_assessment_deadline_absent

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.property_tax_assessment_challenge: A person challenged a tax assessment imposed in respect of property.
predicates.provisional_assessment_payable: The law makes a provisional assessment payable before the property has been regularly assessed.
predicates.assessment_procedure_absent: The law does not prescribe adequate procedures for making and contesting the assessment.
predicates.regular_assessment_deadline_absent: The law sets no ascertainable deadline for completing the survey and regular assessment.

issues.definition: A property-tax assessment scheme unreasonably restricts property rights when a payable provisional assessment lacks adequate procedures and no ascertainable deadline governs regular assessment.
